entries.label: Calls every angle wider than a right angle obtuse
entries.description: The student knows an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but forgets that it must also be smaller than a straight angle, so a straight angle or a reflex angle gets called obtuse.
entries.signal: Answers obtuse angle for a straight line, for an angle of $180^{\circ}$, or for an angle of $210^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You are right that an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle. What is missing is the upper limit: an obtuse angle must also be smaller than a straight angle.
An obtuse angle is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of exactly $180^{\circ}$ is a straight angle: its two sides make one straight line.
Once an angle is bigger than $180^{\circ}$ it is a reflex angle. So an angle of $210^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle, not an obtuse angle, even though it is also wider than a right angle.

Check the size against $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ in turn. Less than $90^{\circ}$ is acute, exactly $90^{\circ}$ is right, between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$ is obtuse, exactly $180^{\circ}$ is straight, and more than $180^{\circ}$ is reflex.

entries.label: Rounds an angle to the nearest right or straight angle
entries.description: The student sees an angle that is close to $90^{\circ}$ or close to a straight line and names it a right angle or a straight angle, instead of checking whether it is exactly that size.
entries.signal: Answers right angle for an angle of $91^{\circ}$, or straight angle for an angle of $210^{\circ}$ or for a bent angle that is nearly flat.

refutation.text_md: You noticed how close the angle is to $90^{\circ}$ (or to a straight line), and comparing with those sizes is the right habit. The slip is treating "close to" as "equal to".
A right angle is exactly $90^{\circ}$, and a straight angle is exactly $180^{\circ}$. An angle that is even one degree more or less is a different type.
An angle of $91^{\circ}$ is bigger than $90^{\circ}$ and smaller than $180^{\circ}$, so it is an obtuse angle, not a right angle.
In the same way, $210^{\circ}$ is more than $180^{\circ}$, so it is a reflex angle, not a straight angle. And two sides that bend, even slightly, do not make a straight line.
So ask two questions: is it exactly $90^{\circ}$? Is it exactly $180^{\circ}$? If not, decide whether it is less than or more than each of them, and name it from that.

entries.label: Names the angle on the unmarked side of the arc
entries.description: The student names the smaller angle between the two lines, on the inside of the bend, instead of the angle the arc actually marks, so a marked reflex angle is called obtuse.
entries.signal: Answers obtuse angle when the arc is drawn round the outside of the bend.

refutation.text_md: Two lines that meet at a point make two angles, one on the inside of the bend and one on the outside. You named the inside one, which really is the smaller angle. The question, though, is about the angle the arc marks.
The arc shows which angle to name. When it is drawn round the outside of the bend, going the long way from one line to the other, the angle it marks is the larger one.
That larger angle is bigger than a straight angle, so it is more than $180^{\circ}$. An angle of more than $180^{\circ}$ is a reflex angle.

Next time, trace the arc with your finger from one line to the other. If it goes the long way round, past a straight line, the angle is a reflex angle. If it stays on the inside, name it by comparing its size with $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

entries.label: Swaps the names acute and obtuse
entries.description: The student judges correctly that one angle is narrow and another is wide, but attaches the names the wrong way round, calling a wide angle acute and a narrow angle obtuse.
entries.signal: Answers acute angle for an angle wider than a right angle, or obtuse angle for an angle narrower than a right angle.

refutation.text_md: You have judged the size correctly: one angle is narrow and the other is wide. It is the names that have been swapped, which is easy to do with two names you have to remember.

Compare with a right angle. An acute angle is narrower than a right angle, so it is smaller than $90^{\circ}$. An obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle, so it is between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.
For example, an angle of $91^{\circ}$ is wider than a right angle, so it is obtuse. Calling it acute would mean it is smaller than $90^{\circ}$.
Before naming an angle, ask one question: is it narrower or wider than a right angle? Narrower is acute. Wider, but not as wide as a straight line, is obtuse.

A human should check them against the book's table of angle types.

The refutations say 'the two sides' and 'the two lines' for the lines that meet at an angle, and 'the arc' for the marker. None of this wording appears in the evidence supplied, so it should be checked against the book's vocabulary. 'Sides' and 'lines' were chosen over 'arms' and 'rays' for that reason.

entries.label: Calls lines parallel because they look it
entries.description: The student answers 'parallel' because the lines look parallel in the picture, or because the angles come out close, even though the angle test does not hold exactly.
entries.signal: Writes that the angles are 'about' or 'nearly' equal, or 'close to' $180^\circ$, and answers parallel.

refutation.text_md: You went by how the lines look, or by the angles coming out close, and called them parallel. That is a natural first reaction, and it was right to look at the angles. The catch is that a drawing can look parallel when it is not.

The test is exact: two lines are parallel only if corresponding angles are equal, alternate interior angles are equal, or co-interior angles add up to exactly $180^\circ$. An angle that misses by a few degrees fails the test, and a few degrees is too small to see in a picture.

For example, co-interior angles of $115^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ add to $115^\circ+55^\circ=170^\circ$. That is not $180^\circ$, so those lines are not parallel, however close they look. In the same way, corresponding angles of $56^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ are not equal, so those lines are not parallel either.

Choose one pair (corresponding, alternate interior or co-interior), find both sizes (using angles on a straight line where you need to), and run the exact test. Answer 'parallel' only when the test holds exactly.

entries.label: Compares the marked angles without matching their positions
entries.description: The student sets the two angle sizes marked on the figure side by side, sees that they differ, and calls the lines not parallel, without first finding the angle that sits in the matching position.

refutation.text_md: You compared the two marked angle sizes, $95^\circ$ and $85^\circ$, saw that they are different, and decided the lines are not parallel. Comparing angle sizes is the right test. The trouble is that these two are not the pair the test asks about.

The test only works on a matching pair: corresponding angles or alternate interior angles (which must be equal), or co-interior angles (which must add to $180^\circ$). Two angles in different positions can differ whether or not the lines are parallel, so their being different tells you nothing.

Here the $95^\circ$ is below the upper line, on the left of the transversal (the line cutting across), and the $85^\circ$ is below the lower line, on the right of it. They are not in matching positions. Use angles on a straight line to reach the matching one: next to the $95^\circ$ is $180^\circ-95^\circ=85^\circ$, which sits below the upper line on the right of the transversal, in the same position as the marked $85^\circ$ at the lower line. Those are corresponding angles, and they are equal.

Before you compare, ask where each angle sits at its own crossing. If it is not in the matching position, use angles on a straight line to move to the one that is, then test. Here the corresponding angles are equal, so the lines are parallel.

entries.label: Expects co-interior angles to be equal
entries.description: The student tests a pair of co-interior angles for being equal, as they would corresponding or alternate angles, finds them different, and decides the lines are not parallel.

refutation.text_md: You tested a pair of co-interior angles for being equal, found they were not, and decided the lines were not parallel. Testing an angle pair is the right idea, and you are right that corresponding angles and alternate interior angles must be equal. Co-interior angles follow a different rule.
Co-interior angles lie between the two lines on the same side of the transversal. If the lines are parallel, they add up to $180^\circ$ (they are supplementary) rather than being equal.

That is why two unequal co-interior angles prove nothing. If they were equal and also added to $180^\circ$, each would be $90^\circ$, so parallel lines give equal co-interior angles only when the transversal meets them at a right angle. Usually one angle is narrower and the other wider, and the pair still passes the test.

entries.label: Adds the squares even when a shorter side is the unknown
entries.description: The student writes $x^2 = a^2 + b^2$ with the two given lengths every time, without checking whether the unknown side is the one opposite the right angle.
entries.signal: An unknown shorter side that comes out longer than the given side opposite the right angle, for example about 13.93 instead of 12 when the given sides are 13 cm and 5 cm.

refutation.text_md: You added the two squares, which is exactly right when $x$ is the side opposite the right angle. The theorem of Pythagoras has a fixed shape, though: the square of the side opposite the right angle stands alone on one side, and the squares of the other two sides are added on the other.

Try it on a right-angled triangle where the side opposite the right angle is 13 cm and another side is 5 cm. Adding gives $x^2 = 13^2 + 5^2 = 194$. Now check that against the theorem: the squares of the two sides next to the right angle should add up to $13^2 = 169$, but $194 + 5^2 = 219$. The answer fails its own check.
Put the side opposite the right angle on its own: $13^2 = x^2 + 5^2$. Then $x^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 144$, so $x = 12$ cm, and now $144 + 25 = 169$ checks.

Before you add or subtract, find the right-angle mark and ask which side is opposite it. If $x$ is that side, add the squares of the other two, as with 15 and 20 giving $x^2 = 625$ and $x = 25$. If $x$ is one of the other two sides, subtract the square of the known short side from the square of the side opposite the right angle.

entries.label: Uses only one of the two equal angles in the angle sum
entries.description: In an isosceles triangle the student knows two angles are equal but writes the angle sum with only one of them, so the unknown angle comes out too big.
entries.signal: Each equal angle comes out as 144 degrees when the angle between the two equal sides is 36 degrees, or 45 degrees when the three angles are $x$, $x$ and $3x$.

refutation.text_md: You spotted that two angles of the isosceles triangle are equal, which is the right start. The slip is in the sum of the angles: a triangle has three angles, so an equal angle has to be written twice, once for each corner it belongs to.

Take an isosceles triangle where the angle between the two equal sides is $36^{\circ}$ and the other two angles are both $x$. Writing $36^{\circ} + x = 180^{\circ}$ gives $x = 144^{\circ}$, and that angle appears at two corners. Check: $36^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} + 144^{\circ} = 324^{\circ}$, far more than the $180^{\circ}$ the angles of a triangle add up to.

With both equal angles in the sum, $180^{\circ} = 36^{\circ} + 2x$, so $2x = 144^{\circ}$. The $144^{\circ}$ is the two equal angles together, so it has to be shared between them: $x = 72^{\circ}$, and $36^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} + 72^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$ checks.

Write one angle per corner in the sum, and let the equal angles appear as many times as there are equal corners. For angles $x$, $x$ and $3x$ that is $x + x + 3x = 180^{\circ}$, so $5x = 180^{\circ}$ and $x = 36^{\circ}$.

entries.label: Puts an angle outside the triangle into the 180 degree sum
entries.description: The student treats an angle that lies outside the triangle, next to a side that has been extended, as the third angle of the triangle and sets the three angles equal to $180^{\circ}$.
entries.signal: An angle marked outside the triangle comes out as $180^{\circ}$ minus the other two angles, for example 82 degrees instead of 98 degrees when the other two angles are 30 degrees and 68 degrees.

refutation.text_md: You used the sum of the angles of a triangle, which is correct for the three angles inside the triangle. The slip is that the angle marked $x$ sits outside the triangle, on the straight line made by extending one side, so it is not the third angle of the triangle.

Take a triangle with $30^{\circ}$ and $68^{\circ}$ inside it and an angle $x$ outside it at the third corner. Then $180^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} - 68^{\circ} = 82^{\circ}$ is the angle inside the triangle at that corner, not $x$. The angle $x$ lies next to it on a straight line, so $x + 82^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$ and $x = 98^{\circ}$.

There is a quicker route for an exterior angle of a triangle: it equals the sum of the two angles inside the triangle at the other two corners. Here $x = 30^{\circ} + 68^{\circ} = 98^{\circ}$, which matches the straight-line check.

Before using $180^{\circ}$, ask whether the angle is inside the triangle. If it is outside, either add the two inside angles at the other corners, or find the angle on the straight line first and then use it. For instance, $y + 68^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$ gives $y = 112^{\circ}$, and then $112^{\circ} = x + 68^{\circ}$ gives $x = 44^{\circ}$.

entries.label: Treating the angles at a meeting point as vertically opposite when the lines are not straight
entries.description: The student sees two triangles touching at a point, assumes the angles there are equal because they are vertically opposite, and uses that angle as the included angle for SAS, even though the lines through the point are not straight lines.

refutation.text_md: You have two pairs of equal sides meeting at a point, and you went looking for the angle between them. That is the right instinct for SAS. The catch is the claim that the angles at that point are equal: vertically opposite angles are only equal when two **straight** lines cross.

If the sides on either side of the point do not carry on in a straight line through it, they are just sides that happen to meet there. The angles between them are not vertically opposite, and nothing given says they are equal, so you cannot use them.
Without that angle, what you really know is two equal sides in each triangle and nothing more. The book says we need at least three facts about the triangles, and two equal sides is only two facts.

Before you write "vertically opposite angles", check that both lines really are straight through the point. If you cannot show that, use only the facts you are given. If they do not complete one of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS, the answer is "not enough information".

entries.label: Treating "not enough information" as "not congruent"
entries.description: The student cannot complete a congruence rule from the facts given, or sees sides with different marks, and concludes the triangles are not congruent, as if a missing fact were proof that they differ.
entries.signal: Answers "not congruent" because no congruence rule can be completed from the facts given, or because the sides carry different marks.

refutation.text_md: You are right that nothing given lets you show these triangles are congruent: no rule from SSS, SAS, AAS and RHS is complete. The slip is the next step. Failing to show that triangles are congruent is not the same as showing that they are not.

"Not enough information" says the facts you have been given leave the question open. We cannot say they are congruent, and we cannot say they are not, because the facts that would settle it have not been given. That is the answer the book gives when a pair of triangles is in this position.

Take two isosceles triangles where the marks only show that two sides **within** each triangle are equal. No side of one triangle is said to equal a side of the other, so we are not given any equal sides across the two triangles. Different marks on the sides only mean the sides are not stated to be equal. They do not state that the sides are different.

List the facts you are given, one pair at a time, and compare them with SSS, SAS, AAS and RHS. If a rule is complete, write the congruence with its reason. If none is, answer "not enough information" and say which fact is missing, for example that no side is known to be equal across the two triangles.

entries.label: Reading equal sides inside each triangle as equal sides between the triangles
entries.description: The student sees a pair of equal sides marked in each triangle and treats them as if a side of one triangle were equal to a side of the other, then adds a pair of equal angles and calls the triangles congruent.

refutation.text_md: You have spotted that each triangle has a pair of equal sides marked, and that is a real fact: each triangle is isosceles. But what those marks say is that two sides of the **same** triangle are equal. They do not say that a side of one triangle equals a side of the other.

A congruence rule needs facts that link the two triangles. In a pair where congruence can be shown, the same mark appears on one side of each triangle, so the mark pairs a side from one triangle with a side from the other. Marks inside a single triangle cannot be matched against the other triangle.

Equal angles do not rescue it. You may be able to work out which angles are equal, but each of SSS, SAS, AAS and RHS needs at least one pair of equal sides, one side from each triangle, and none is given.

For every mark, ask which two sides it joins. If both sides are in the same triangle, it only tells you the triangle is isosceles. Count only the facts that link a side or angle of one triangle to the other. If those do not complete a rule, answer "not enough information".

entries.label: Writing the letters of a congruence statement in the wrong order
entries.description: The student finds the right pair of triangles and the right rule, but writes the letters of one triangle in an order that does not line up with the matching corners of the other.

refutation.text_md: You have found the right pair of triangles and probably the right rule. The slip is in how the letters are written. In a congruence statement the letters are not just names: their order says which corner matches which, first with first, second with second, third with third.

Take one triangle with $90^\circ$ at $D$, $35^\circ$ at $C$ and $55^\circ$ at $E$, and another with $90^\circ$ at $B$, $35^\circ$ at $C$ and $55^\circ$ at $A$. The equal corners are $D$ with $B$, $C$ with $C$ and $E$ with $A$. Written in that order the statement is $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle CBA$.
Change the order and the statement says something false. $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle ABC$ would pair $C$, which is $35^\circ$, with $A$, which is $55^\circ$, and those angles are not equal.

The order also does work afterwards. From $\triangle CDE\equiv\triangle CBA$ you can read straight off that $CE=CA$, because $C$ and $E$ sit in the same places as $C$ and $A$. To write your own statement, pair up the equal angles and sides first, then write each triangle's letters in that same pairing order, and check that the first letters match, then the second, then the third.

flags.text: I avoided the term "tick marks" and wrote "marks" / "marked as equal", because the book's own wording in these solutions is "marked as equal" and "indicated by" and I could not confirm it uses "ticks".

I wrote "matching corners" and "matches" for corresponding vertices. The book uses "corresponding" for sides (in one worked example) but I have not seen it define corresponding corners, so a human may want to swap in "corresponding" in the letter-order entry.

The re-solve note says the triangles are "only similar". I did not use similarity: it is outside this objective and the book does not teach it here. I used only the re-solve's wrong turn (answering "not congruent"), and treated it as our own check, not the book's.

The letter-order entry has no wrong option attached. It rests on the book's printed caution about order of letters and the worked example whose angles and sides I described in words. I found no evidence in the questions or sources for a rule-choice error (for example using SAS with a non-included angle), so I wrote no entry for it.

entries.label: Calls a pair similar without matching the angle markers
entries.description: The student picks the pair of triangles that looks alike, or whose corners simply carry marks, without checking that each marker on one triangle is repeated on the corresponding corner of the other.

refutation.text_md: You chose the pair that looks like the same shape, or whose corners carry marks. Marked angles are exactly the right place to look, and a first impression is a fair start. What is still missing is the comparison: a drawing can look alike and still have different angles, so how it looks cannot decide the question.

The AAA rule asks for corresponding angles that are equal. In a diagram, equal angles carry the same marker: the same number of arcs, or the same letter. Two arcs and three arcs are different markers, so they stand for different angles, however alike the triangles look.

Take a pair where one triangle has a corner with two arcs and a corner with one arc, and the other triangle has a corner with three arcs and a corner with four arcs. Both triangles have marks at the matching corners, but no marker on one is repeated on the other. The angles are all different, so no pair of corresponding angles is equal and the triangles are not similar. The same goes for letters: corners called $a$, $b$, $c$ in one triangle and $d$, $e$, $f$ in the other share no marker, so none of the angles is shown equal.

So set the look of the triangles aside and go corner by corner. A pair of triangles is similar when the corresponding angles carry the same markers, and the pair where the same markers appear on both triangles is the one to choose.

entries.label: Accepts sides that grow by different amounts as in proportion
entries.description: The student sees that every side of the bigger triangle is a larger multiple of the matching side of the smaller one and calls the triangles similar, without checking that it is the same multiple for all three pairs of sides.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that every side of the bigger triangle is a longer version of the matching side of the smaller one, and that is the right thing to look at first. The check still to do is whether each side grew by the same amount.
The SSS rule needs the three pairs of corresponding sides to be in proportion. Comparing each bigger side with its matching smaller side has to give the same result all three times.

Take a small triangle with sides $x$, $y$, $z$ and a larger one with sides $2.3x$, $2.5y$, $2.2z$. Every side has grown to more than twice its length, but the three sides are $2.3$ times, $2.5$ times and $2.2$ times as long. Those are three different amounts, so the sides are not in proportion and the triangles are not similar.

Compare a larger triangle with sides $1.2x$, $1.2y$, $1.2z$. Each side is $1.2$ times the matching side, the same amount every time, so the three pairs of sides are in proportion and the triangles are similar.
So work out the comparison for each of the three pairs of matching sides, and call the triangles similar only when all three agree.

entries.label: Writes the letters of similar triangles out of corresponding order
entries.description: The student names the second triangle with its letters in a different order from the corners that correspond to the first, so the statement pairs the wrong corners and sides.
entries.signal: A similarity statement in which the letters of the second triangle are in a different order from the matching corners, such as $\triangle MNL|||\triangle RTS$ where $\triangle MNL|||\triangle RST$ is correct.

refutation.text_md: You have the right two triangles, and you have seen that they are similar. The slip is in the order of the letters: the second triangle's letters were written in the order you came across them, as if the order did not matter. The book says similar triangles must always be labelled in corresponding order.

The order carries information. The letters in the same position name corresponding corners: the first letter of one triangle goes with the first letter of the other, the second with the second, the third with the third. That is how a reader knows which angles are equal and which sides are in proportion.

Look at the book's own pair of statements. $\triangle MNL|||\triangle RST$ is correct, but $\triangle MNL|||\triangle RTS$ is incorrect. Both use the same six letters, yet the first says $M$ goes with $R$, $N$ with $S$ and $L$ with $T$, while the second says $N$ goes with $T$ and $L$ with $S$. Swapping two letters changes the statement from correct to incorrect.

The order matters again when you write the sides as fractions. In $\triangle MNL|||\triangle RST$, the side $MN$ goes with the side $RS$, because $M$ goes with $R$ and $N$ goes with $S$. It does not go with $RT$.

So before you write the statement, match up the equal angles, then write the second triangle's letters in the order of their matching corners. Read the statement back position by position and check that each pair of letters names corners that are equal.

entries.label: Thinks AAA needs all three pairs of angles shown equal
entries.description: The student will not accept a pair of triangles as similar by AAA unless all three pairs of angles are marked equal, so a pair with only two matching markers is rejected or left undecided.

refutation.text_md: The name AAA does suggest three angles, and you are right that similar triangles need all three pairs of corresponding angles equal. What you do not need is to be shown the third pair: two matching markers already settle it.
The angles in a triangle always add up to $180^{\circ}$. So the third angle in each triangle is what is left when the other two angles are taken away from $180^{\circ}$.

If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of the other, the same amount is taken away from $180^{\circ}$ in both triangles, so what is left must be the same in both. The third pair of angles is equal even though it carries no marker: the third angle in each triangle must be equal.

So when two corners of one triangle carry the same markers as the matching two corners of the other, treat all three pairs of angles as equal and call the triangles similar by AAA. Check that the two markers really match one for one.

flags.text: I used 'angle markers' for both the arcs and the letters a, b, c, following the wording of the book's solutions ('the same three angle markers are shown in both triangles'). I also say 'arcs' for the arc marks; I am not certain 'arcs' is the book's own word for them. Please confirm both terms.

I said 'in proportion' and 'corresponding order', which are the book's own phrases, and the book's similarity symbol |||. I deliberately avoided 'scale factor' and 'ratio' and wrote 'times' and 'comparing each pair of matching sides' instead, because I could not confirm the book uses those terms for this objective.

The canonical solution for the question asking why triangle PQR is similar to triangle TSR concludes with 'PQR ||| TRS' (Rs and Ss swapped). That contradicts the book's own caution about corresponding order, because P corresponds to T, Q to S and R to R. I did not use this solution in any refutation. It needs a human check.

The worked example on triangles ABC and DEF prints 'DF/AC = 32/64 = 9/16' in its canonical solution, but the figure shows DF = 36 (36/64 = 9/16, whereas 32/64 = 1/2). It looks like a mis-transcription. I did not use this example's numbers, and used it only as a source for the idea of three pairs of sides in proportion.

The canonical solution for the first AAA question says 'the same three angle markers are shown in both triangles', but its figure marks only two angles in each triangle (the third corner is unmarked). The conclusion is unaffected. Entry aaa-needs-three-marked is written for exactly that situation.

All four wrong options are simply the other diagram in a two-option question, so none records a student's reasoning. The assignments rest on how the book drew the non-similar diagram (arcs two and one against three and four; sides $2.3x$, $2.5y$, $2.2z$; letters a to c against d to f). The assignment of D3 is the least secure. The letter-order caution and the two-angles-are-enough remark are not encoded by any wrong option here, so those two entries have no distractor assigned.
The book's figures print decimal commas (for example 2,3x). I wrote them with a decimal point (2.3x) to match the app's notation.

entries.label: Reads 'bisect each other' as 'the diagonals are equal'
entries.description: The student takes 'the diagonals bisect each other' to mean the two diagonals are the same length (or meet at right angles), sees that this is not what a parallelogram guarantees, and so rejects the statement instead of checking that each diagonal is cut in half at the point where they cross.

refutation.text_md: Choosing False often comes from reading "bisect each other" as "the two diagonals are equal in length" (or "they cross at right angles"). Your instinct that bisecting is about equal lengths is right, but the equal lengths are the two halves of each diagonal, not one diagonal compared with the other.

Test it on a parallelogram $MNRS$ whose diagonals $MR$ and $NS$ cross at $P$. In $\triangle MNP$ and $\triangle RSP$: $\hat{M}_1=\hat{R}_1$ (alternate angles, $MN\parallel SR$), $\hat{P}_1=\hat{P}_3$ (vertically opposite angles) and $MN=RS$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram). So $\triangle MNP\equiv\triangle RSP$ (AAS).
Congruent triangles give $MP=RP$, so $P$ is the mid-point of $MR$. In the same way $\triangle MSP\equiv\triangle RNP$ (AAS), which gives $NP=SP$, so $P$ is also the mid-point of $NS$.

Each diagonal is cut into two equal halves by the other, at the same point $P$. That is exactly what "bisect each other" says. The proof never compares the length of $MR$ with the length of $NS$ and never uses the size of the angle at $P$, so the statement does not depend on either.

Next time you meet "the diagonals bisect each other", do not ask whether the diagonals are equal. Ask whether the crossing point is the mid-point of each one, and check it with the two pairs of congruent triangles (alternate angles, vertically opposite angles, opposite sides of a parallelogram). Here the answer is True.

flags.text: The only evidence for this entry is the wrong option 'False' on a true/false item. The book prints no caution or remark, and no re-solve evidence was supplied. Why a student picks False is my inference (reading 'bisect' as 'equal' or 'perpendicular'), not something the book flags. A human reviewer should confirm it is worth keeping; if not, assign D0 to '' and let the runtime fall back to the canonical solution.

The book's solutions say 'bisect one another / bisect each other' and 'P is the mid-point of MR', but the evidence gives no definition of 'bisect'. The refutation explains it only through the book's 'mid-point' wording ('cut into two equal halves'). Please confirm that wording.

The book abbreviates reasons as 'alt angles', 'vert opp angles' and 'opp sides of parallelogram'. I wrote them out as 'alternate angles', 'vertically opposite angles' and 'opposite sides of a parallelogram'. Confirm these match the spelled-out terms the book uses.

I did not use the angle-chasing questions (parallelogram PQRS with PS=OS and QO=QR; the isosceles triangle with mid-points S, T, U). Possible errors the questions suggest but the evidence does not support, left out on purpose: (1) treating the given equal diagonals (AC = BD in the diagonals question, where the figure looks like a rectangle) as the reason the quadrilateral is a parallelogram, when the book's solution uses only that the diagonals bisect each other; (2) using the angle-sum argument without showing the opposite angles are given equal. If a re-solve or a wrong option later shows either, they could be added with the usual evidence.

The book's solutions abbreviate their reasons: 'diag of ∥m', 'Midpt Theorem', 'opp sides of quad are ∥', 'co-interior angles', 'sum of ∠s in a quad'. No entry quotes them, so nothing was changed, but any later entry should keep the book's wording and have a human check these abbreviations.

entries.label: Gives the rhombus the rectangle's equal diagonals
entries.description: The student carries the true fact that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length over to the rhombus and treats the diagonals of a rhombus as equal too.
entries.signal: Marks the statement that the diagonals of a rhombus are equal in length as true.

refutation.text_md: You are carrying a true fact over to the wrong shape. The diagonals of a rectangle really are equal in length, and a rectangle and a rhombus look alike enough that it is easy to hand one shape the other's diagonal facts. Remembering the rectangle fact is right; it just belongs to the rectangle.

See where the rectangle's equal diagonals come from. In rectangle $PQRS$, the triangles $PSR$ and $QRS$ share the side $SR$, have $PS=QR$ (opposite sides of a rectangle), and both have a $90^{\circ}$ angle at a corner. That makes them congruent by RHS, so the diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ are equal. The whole proof leans on the corners being $90^{\circ}$.

A rhombus only promises that all four sides are equal. Nothing makes its corners $90^{\circ}$, so the RHS argument has no right angle to stand on. Try a rhombus where a diagonal splits one corner into two angles of $65^{\circ}$ each: that corner is $130^{\circ}$, so the shape is not a rectangle. The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, and bisecting diagonals that are also equal would make the shape a rectangle. So the diagonals of this rhombus cannot be equal.

What a rhombus does give you is different: its diagonals bisect each other at right angles (proved with $\triangle XTO\equiv\triangle ZTO$ by SSS) and bisect the interior angles. When a question is about a rhombus, use those. The centre angle is $90^{\circ}$, so the other two angles of that triangle add up to $90^{\circ}$. Keep "the diagonals are equal" for the rectangle.

flags.text: No caution boxes, worked-example remarks or re-solve wrong turns were supplied for this objective. The single entry rests on the wrong option 'True' (D0), supported by the book's rectangle proof (equal diagonals via RHS) and rhombus proof (diagonals bisect at right angles and bisect the interior angles via SSS).

Step 3 uses the book's reasoning for identifying a rectangle: bisecting diagonals that are equal make the quadrilateral a rectangle. That comes from the terse worked solution to the 'prove ABCD is a rectangle' item, where the book's only reason is 'diags of rectangle'. Please confirm this is the converse the book intends.

Step 3's 65-degree corner comes from the book's answer x = 15 in the rhombus angle question (3x+20 = 65), combined with the book's property that diagonals bisect the interior angles. The book itself does not compute the 130-degree corner.

Terms used as the book words them: 'bisect each other perpendicularly / at right angles', 'bisect the interior angles', 'opposite sides of rectangle', 'RHS', 'SSS'. The word 'square' is deliberately not used, because the book's solution says rhombus diagonals are not equal and does not treat the square as a special case.

entries.label: Doubts that a kite's diagonals cross at right angles
entries.description: The student says the diagonals of a kite do not intersect at right angles, treating the right angle as something a lopsided shape like a kite cannot have.
entries.signal: Answers 'False' to a statement that the diagonals of a kite intersect at right angles.

refutation.text_md: You answered False, as if the diagonals of a kite could not cross at a right angle. A kite looks lopsided, so a right angle there is easy to doubt, but it is a property of every kite and it can be proved.

Take a kite $ABCD$ with $AD=AB$ and $CD=CB$, and let the diagonals meet at $O$. Diagonal $AC$ lies between the equal sides, so it bisects $\hat{A}$: $B\hat{A}O=D\hat{A}O$. Triangles $ADO$ and $ABO$ then have $AD=AB$, the side $AO$ in common, and these equal angles at $A$, so they are congruent (SAS). That gives $A\hat{B}O=A\hat{D}O$.

Call each of the equal angles at $A$ by the letter $t$, and call $A\hat{B}O=A\hat{D}O$ by the letter $p$. The angles of triangle $ADB$ add up to $180^\circ$, so $2t+2p=180^\circ$, which gives $t+p=90^\circ$.

Now $A\hat{O}D$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABO$, so it equals the two opposite interior angles added together: $A\hat{O}D=A\hat{B}O+B\hat{A}O=p+t=90^\circ$. So $AC\perp BD$: the diagonals of a kite do intersect at $90^\circ$, and the statement is True.

Whenever you doubt this property, check it the same way: mark the equal sides, bisect the angle between them, prove the two small triangles congruent, and use the angle sum to show the angle at the crossing point is $t+p=90^\circ$.

entries.label: Gives both diagonals of a kite the angle-bisecting job
entries.description: The student knows the diagonal between the equal sides bisects the interior angles, and wrongly decides that both diagonals of a kite do this.
entries.signal: Answers 'True' to a statement that both diagonals of a kite bisect the interior angles.

refutation.text_md: You said both diagonals of a kite bisect the interior angles. Part of that is right: the diagonal between the equal sides does bisect the interior angles at its two ends. The slip is to give the other diagonal the same job.

Take a kite $ABCD$ with $AD=AB$ and $CD=CB$. Diagonal $AC$ lies between the equal sides. Triangles $ADC$ and $ABC$ have $AD=AB$, $CD=CB$ and $AC$ in common, so they are congruent (SSS). Their matching angles are equal, so $AC$ bisects $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{C}$.

Try the same proof for diagonal $BD$. Triangles $ABD$ and $CBD$ would have to be congruent, which needs $AB=CB$ and $AD=CD$. A kite only gives $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$, so the SSS argument that works for $AC$ gives nothing for $BD$. What is true at $B$ and $D$ is different: $A\hat{D}C=A\hat{B}C$, one pair of opposite angles are equal to each other, which is not the same as being bisected.

So the statement is False: only one diagonal of a kite bisects one pair of interior angles. When you see 'both diagonals', ask which diagonal lies between the equal sides. Only that one bisects the angles at its ends.

flags.text: The book abbreviates 'exterior angle of a triangle' as 'ext angle of triangle' and 'sum of angles in a triangle' as 'sum of angles in triangle'; the entries write them in full words ('exterior angle', 'angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees'). Please confirm that wording matches what the class uses.

No caution box, worked-example remark or re-solve wrong turn was supplied for this objective. Both entries rest only on the deliberately written wrong options, and the student reasoning behind the first (why a student would call the right-angle statement False) is inferred, not documented.

The first refutation re-uses the book's own proof of perpendicular diagonals, but with letters (A, B, C, D, O, and t and p) defined in the text itself so a student who cannot see the book's figure can follow it. The book's version labels the angle at O differently; the content is unchanged.

entries.label: Gives a true but less specific name
entries.description: Asked for the most specific name, the student gives a broader name that is true of the shape (quadrilateral, parallelogram, trapezium or kite) and stops checking before the narrowest name that fits.
entries.signal: The answer is a broader name (quadrilateral, parallelogram, trapezium or kite) where a narrower name also fits the shape.

refutation.text_md: The name you gave really does describe this shape, so you were right as far as you went. The slip is stopping there: a question like this wants the most specific name, and a broad name can be true while saying less than the shape's properties allow.

Broad names fit a lot of shapes, which is exactly why they are the least specific. Every four-sided shape is a quadrilateral. A rectangle, a rhombus and a square all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so all three are parallelograms too.

Take a shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel, all four angles equal to $90^\circ$, and sides that are not all equal in length. 'Quadrilateral' and 'parallelogram' are both true of it, but neither mentions the right angles. The name that carries all of its properties is rectangle.

Keep running the checks until one fails, and answer with the name from the last check you passed. Are both pairs of opposite sides parallel? Are all the angles $90^\circ$? Are all the sides equal? If no opposite sides are parallel, ask whether both pairs of adjacent sides are equal: if they are, the shape is a kite, which is more specific than quadrilateral. Bring the broader names back only when a question asks you to list every name.

entries.label: Thinks a shape can have only one name
entries.description: The student treats rectangle, square, rhombus, parallelogram and kite as separate boxes, so says a rectangle or a square is not a parallelogram, or a rhombus is not a kite, instead of seeing that a shape with extra properties still belongs to the broader group.
entries.signal: Calls a statement such as 'a rectangle is a parallelogram', 'a square is a parallelogram' or 'a rhombus is a kite' false, or lists only the single most specific name when asked for all the names of a shape.

refutation.text_md: You're treating each name as its own box, so that a shape can only be one thing. That's a fair first instinct, because the usual pictures of these shapes look so different from one another. But a name is really a list of properties, and a shape belongs to every group whose list it satisfies.

A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. A rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel too, so it passes the parallelogram test, and then it adds one extra property: all its interior angles are $90^\circ$. A square passes the same test in the same way. Each is a parallelogram with something extra.

The same goes for kite and rhombus. A kite needs two pairs of adjacent sides that are equal in length. A rhombus has all four sides equal, so both of its pairs of adjacent sides are equal and it passes the kite test. It is a kite that also has a pair of equal opposite sides.
A square shows how far this goes: it passes the tests for rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite and quadrilateral, so every one of those names applies to it as well as 'square'.

When a statement says one shape 'is' another, don't ask whether it looks like the usual picture of that shape. Ask whether it passes that shape's test. If it does, the statement is true. When you are asked to list all the names, test each name in turn and keep every one the shape passes.

entries.label: Names a trapezium or a kite without checking its property
entries.description: The student picks trapezium or kite for a shape that does not pass that name's test, because the shape as a whole seems to suit the name, without checking for a pair of parallel opposite sides or for two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
entries.signal: Trapezium for a shape with no parallel sides, or kite for a shape that does not have two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

refutation.text_md: You picked a special name because the shape as a whole seemed to fit it, and that is a sensible place to start. But a special name has to be earned by a property: each one comes with something you can check, and the shape has to pass that check.

A trapezium needs a pair of opposite sides that are parallel. To test it, make a quick sketch and extend each pair of opposite sides: lines that meet at a point are not parallel. If both pairs meet, the shape has no parallel sides, so it cannot be a trapezium.

A kite needs two pairs of adjacent sides, meaning sides that meet at a corner, with the two sides in each pair equal in length. Compare the lengths of the sides that meet at each corner: if they are not equal in two pairs, it is not a kite.

So a four-sided shape with no parallel sides and no equal sides passes neither test, and the only name that fits is quadrilateral. And a shape whose two pairs of adjacent sides are equal, but whose opposite sides are not parallel, is a kite, not a trapezium.
Before you name a shape, run the tests in order. Is any pair of opposite sides parallel? If not, are both pairs of adjacent sides equal? A shape that passes neither is only a quadrilateral.

entries.label: Mixes up what makes a rectangle, a rhombus and a square
entries.description: The student has the family right (four sides, both pairs of opposite sides parallel) but lets right angles and equal sides stand in for each other or hangs them on the wrong name, so a right-angled shape with unequal sides becomes a square or a rhombus, an equal-sided shape with no right angles becomes a square or a rectangle, or the adjacent sides of a rhombus are allowed to differ.
entries.signal: Square for a shape whose sides are not all equal or whose angles are not all $90^\circ$; rhombus for a shape with right angles and unequal sides; rectangle for a shape with four equal sides and no right angles; or 'true' for 'two adjacent sides of a rhombus have different lengths'.

refutation.text_md: You have the family right: four sides, with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. The mix-up is in the two checks that sort that family: 'are all the interior angles $90^\circ$?' and 'are all the sides equal in length?'. They are two separate questions, so one cannot stand in for the other, and each name uses them in its own way.

A rectangle has all four angles equal to $90^\circ$, but its sides do not have to be equal, so it can be long and thin. A rhombus has all four sides equal, so any two sides that meet at a corner are equal in length too, but its angles do not have to be $90^\circ$, so it can lean over.

A square is the shape that answers yes to both questions. A shape with four right angles but sides of two different lengths answers no to the second, so it is a rectangle, not a square and not a rhombus. A shape with four equal sides but no right angles answers no to the first, so it is a rhombus, not a square and not a rectangle.

Ask both questions every time and write down the two answers before you name the shape. All angles $90^\circ$ and sides not all equal gives rectangle. Angles not $90^\circ$ and all sides equal gives rhombus. Yes to both gives square.

stripped.reason: no named error: The honest error is confusing trapezium with parallelogram (two pairs versus a pair of parallel sides), but the book is not consistent here: it says a trapezium has only one pair, yet lists a square and a rhombus as trapeziums. A refutation risks contradicting the book, so this is left to the canonical solution.

flags.text: Trapezium: the book is not consistent. One True/False solution says a trapezium 'only has one pair of opposite parallel sides', yet other solutions list a square and a rhombus as trapeziums because they have 'a pair of opposite sides which are parallel'. I wrote only 'a pair of opposite sides that are parallel' and never 'only one pair' or 'at least one pair'; a human should confirm which reading the book intends before more trapezium copy is written.

Adjacent sides: I glossed it in the student text as 'sides that meet at a corner'. The gloss is mine, not the book's wording; the book uses 'adjacent sides' and 'two pairs of adjacent sides which are the same lengths' for a kite.
Interior angles: the book says 'interior angles are 90 degrees'; I wrote $90^\circ$ in the app's notation.

No caution, remark or re-solve evidence was supplied. Every entry rests on the wrong options plus the canonical solutions. Most options are the book's full list of shape names rather than distractors someone wrote to catch a specific error, so the mapping of options to errors is my inference, not something the book flags.

The question where the student lists all the names of an unmarked four-sided shape shows a single listed answer (quadrilateral). I treated trapezium and kite as wrong there because the solution says the shape has no special properties and is 'only a quadrilateral'.

For the question about the quadrilateral formed by joining mid-points, the options parallelogram, kite, trapezium and quadrilateral are all true names of a rhombus under the book's own definitions. I treated them as true but less specific, not as false; the solution itself only states rhombus.
D10 (trapezium defined with two pairs of parallel sides, marked True) is left unassigned; see the assignment reason.

The area question (finding the area of the composite shape using a rhombus and rectangle) and the compound-figure naming questions have no wrong options or evidence, so no entry was written for the 'solve a problem such as finding an area' part of the objective.

entries.label: Assuming any line across a triangle is parallel to the third side
entries.description: The student sees a line joining two sides of a triangle and takes it to be parallel to the third side, without checking that both of its end points are mid-points of their sides.
entries.signal: Names the line across the triangle and the third side as a pair of parallel lines in a triangle where the points on the sides are not both marked as mid-points.

refutation.text_md: You saw a line drawn from one side of the triangle to another and took it to be parallel to the third side. That is a fair thing to suspect, because the mid-point theorem does say that some lines across a triangle are parallel to the third side. But it says so for one special kind of line only.

The theorem is about the line that joins the **mid-points** of two sides. Each end of the line has to sit exactly halfway along its side. Having both ends on the sides is not enough, and neither is the line looking close to parallel.

Now check the two points in this triangle. Nothing makes either of them the mid-point of its side: the line does not bisect the two sides it meets. So the mid-point theorem gives no reason for it to be parallel to the third side, and the answer is that there are no parallel lines.

Compare a triangle where each of the two sides is cut into two equal parts, with matching tick marks showing the halves. There both points are mid-points, so the line joining them is parallel to the third side, and you can name that pair of parallel lines.
So before you name any parallel lines, ask about each point: is it the mid-point of its side? If both are, the line across is parallel to the third side. If not, there are no parallel lines to name.

flags.text: The refutation says "matching tick marks" for the marks that show two parts of a side are equal. The book's solution text for these questions does not use that phrase (the marks appear only in its figures), so a human should confirm the wording.
The only caution in the evidence says GeoGebra can be used to show that the converse of the mid-point theorem is true. It describes a tool, not a student error, so no entry rests on it.

The evidence offers no wrong turn or option for the converse (a line through a mid-point parallel to a second side bisects the third side), nor for the corresponding-angle and half-length steps. I wrote no entries for them, because I could not name an error that the evidence supports.

entries.label: Puts the factor of 2 on the wrong segment
entries.description: The student compares the right two segments but uses the 2:1 ratio the wrong way round: doubling the line joining the mid-points when it should be halved from the third side, or halving the third side when it should be doubled.
entries.signal: The answer is four times too big or four times too small, as if the long and short segments had swapped places.

refutation.text_md: You picked the right two segments to compare: the line joining the mid-points of two sides, and the third side of the triangle. The slip is in which of the two is the long one, so the factor of 2 ended up on the wrong segment.

The mid-point theorem says the line joining the mid-points is half the length of the third side. Said the other way round, the third side is twice as long as that line, a ratio of $2:1$. The third side is the long one and the line inside the triangle is the short one.

Check it with a case. If the third side is $6$ and the line joining the mid-points is $x$, then $6=2x$, so $x=\tfrac12\times 6=3$. Doubling instead would give $12$, a line inside the triangle that is longer than the side it is half of, which cannot be right.

It works the same the other way. If the line joining the mid-points is $3$ and you need the third side, then third side $=2\times 3=6$. Halving would give $1.5$, a third side shorter than the line inside it.

Before you calculate, write it as $\text{third side}=2\times(\text{line joining the mid-points})$ and put the given length in the right place. Then solve, and check that the third side comes out bigger than the line inside.

entries.label: Uses the mid-point theorem on a segment that does not join mid-points
entries.description: The student treats any segment drawn inside a triangle as the line joining two mid-points and halves or doubles a length, without checking that the points are marked as mid-points or that the segment is parallel to the third side and half its length.

refutation.text_md: You saw a segment inside a triangle with a length on it and reached for the mid-point theorem. That is a sensible first thought, because it is the theorem this topic uses. But the theorem only speaks about a line that joins the mid-points of two sides, so the first job is to check that this is what the picture shows.

Look for the evidence. Either the two parts of each side are marked as equal, or the question tells you the points are mid-points. Or the segment is parallel to the third side and exactly half its length: for example, a parallel segment of length $5$ under a side of length $10$ tells you its end points are the mid-points of the other two sides.

If neither is there, the theorem has nothing to say. In a triangle where the segment inside is not parallel to the third side and nothing is marked as equal, the book's conclusion is that the mid-point theorem cannot apply, so the question has no solution. Halving or doubling the given lengths anyway still produces a number, but the number has no justification.

Before you use the theorem, ask two questions. Are the points marked or stated as mid-points? If not, is the segment parallel to the third side and exactly half of it? If one answer is yes, go ahead and use the theorem. If both are no, say that the theorem does not apply.

flags.text: The evidence block was empty: no caution box, no worked-example remark list, no re-solve wrong turns, no wrong options, no existing entries. Both entries rest only on text inside the question file itself: the book's own reminder in its solutions that the third side is twice as long as the line joining the mid-points (for the 2:1 entry), and the book's own teaching item where the theorem is declared not to apply because the segment is not parallel (for the conditions entry). A reviewer may reasonably decide these are too thin and drop either one; the runtime then falls back to the canonical solution.

Not used, for lack of evidence: halving or doubling only the first term of a two-term expression such as $-2a+4$ or $\tfrac{2a}{3}+4$, which is a likely error on the variable questions but has no caution, remark or option behind it here.
